articles.title: Misunderstanding Pakistan
articles.content: THE foundational basis of Pakistan and the objectives behind the country’s creation remain a subject of debate. One side emphasises religion above all else and argues that the basis for creating Pakistan was Islam itself. On the other hand, some commentators contend that Pakistan was created for the residents of specific regions, the majority of whom were Muslims, so that they could live their lives freely and without subjugation. Although religion was undeniably important, the primary goal was to secure the people’s free will and freedom. Even without debating which worldview is accurate — if any — we can agree on a few truths. First, Pakistan was born through the will and struggle of its people. Second, the decision to create Pakistan was achieved and affirmed through their votes. And finally, Pakistan was brought into being through a process that can, arguably, be considered democratic. In essence, the establishment of Pakistan was people-centric. And when the ‘people’ in question share a single culture, language, history, and geography, it becomes easy to categorise them as a monolithic community with a singular identity. However, when a nation comprises diverse ethnic groups with distinct cultures and histories running parallel to one another, neatly situated in separate regions of a land seeking to unite, the mechanics of political representation necessarily change. Unlike a single monolithic community represented by a unitary voice, multiple distinct communities seeking union often have separate representatives, at least initially, to protect their specific interests within the broader polity. The union is not the merging of a single people, but a voluntary arrangement among distinct communities with shared goals. To achieve this, these communities, through their representatives, discuss, negotiate, and agree on the union’s dynamics, defining which powers are transferred to the central state and which remain local. Commentators frequently overlook the foundational premise of the nation itself. This process transfers sovereignty from individual communities to a united entity that becomes greater than the sum of its parts, while protecting regional rights and identities. The goal of such a union is a better shared future; unity is seen as offering greater benefits than division. This fusion of distinct groups into a singular national framework is the essence of entering into a social contract. Pakistan, which is home to diverse ethnicities and communities, is said to have entered into precisely this type of union right after independence. For many, that social contract was earlier epitomised by the Lahore Resolution of 1940; for others, it was crystallised in the 1973 Constitution. Whichever document one examines, the formal recognition and celebration of diversity are recurring themes. Pakistan was always intended to be pluralistic, with communities coming together to pool their resources and cede certain freedoms for the collective good. Pakistan came into being for them, not despite them. Abdul Wali Khan articulated well the vision of what Pakistan could be, noting that despite their distinct identities, the federating units were akin to “flowers with their distinct colours and fragrance” that “blend into a bouquet, manifesting their unity in diversity”. Ultimately, the country’s founding idea is rooted in protecting its people, their cultures, languages, and rights. That is what it ought to be, and whether anyone likes it or not, this is what it was always meant to be. Why is this discussion so critical today? Because when commentators debate whether creating more provinces is necessary for a prosperous Pakistan, whether local governments need to be strengthened, or whether addressing the missing persons issue is key to winning hearts and minds, they frequently overlook the foundational premise of the nation itself. This premise is intrinsically linked to the people’s will and aspirations. As with any major decision, altering provincial boundaries, whether by creating fewer or more provinces or restructuring existing ones, must remain a choice driven directly by the people whose goals are bound to Pakistan’s genesis. Similarly, the people must decide the role of local governments, and the resolution of the missing persons crisis must be as great a priority as the people make it. If you remove the popular will from this decision-making process, you strike at the core of Pakistan’s founding identity. You not only carve up administrative boundaries and dismiss popularly held convictions, but also dismember the very vision articulated in the 1940 Resolution, codified in the 1973 Constitution, and reaffirmed through the 18th Amendment. Democracy is neither a luxury that Pakistan cannot afford nor is it a failed concept. If anything, when allowed to function, democratic governance is the single thread that has kept this federation together throughout its turbulent history. It maintains the vital link between the state and the populace that gave it birth. If new administrative units are to be carved out or other consequential decisions to be taken, those decisions belong exclusively to the public, not to self-appointed arbiters who claim to know better than the citizens themselves. After all, armies did not create Pakistan; the people’s vote did. War tacticians did not envision Pakistan; politicians, lawyers, and civilians did. A war did not lead the nation to independence; a barrister did. Consequently, the bond between the Pakistani state and its citizens is as intrinsic and consequential as water is to fish, instruments are to musicians, and ‘national interest’ is to our armed forces. If you remove the people from decision-making, you strip away the soul of the country. What remains is merely a land without a people, a people without a voice, and a country without a purpose, with nothing left but despair.
articles.author: Basil Nabi Malik

articles.title: Refinery upgradation plans
articles.content: AFTER a full year of criticism that while it had stabilised the economy it had offered no vision for reform, the government is finally moving. A string of recent announcements makes the reform path clearer. Refineries are being asked to upgrade their operations in return for concessions granted in the Brownfield Refinery Upgradation Policy. A number of power distribution companies are being prepared for privatisation, and the ministry has announced the beginning of power wheeling, an important reform stuck in limbo since 2017 and an essential plank in any effort to reform power pricing. The finance ministry is helping arrange resources for the refineries and the newly privatised PIA, as well as moving along the commitments for the Reko Diq project. A meeting between the finance minister and officials from the US Exim Bank was wrongly interpreted by many as an effort by the government to borrow on behalf of the newly privatised PIA for aircraft procurement. It turned out to be nothing of the sort. Meanwhile, March saw a spectrum auction, setting the stage for the rollout of 5G telecommunications in Pakistan; unlike the last auction in 2021, which saw a lacklustre response, three large telecoms participated and picked up spectrum at a price tag of $500 million. So things are finally beginning to move on the structural front. Obviously, it is too early to call the results, but if the envisioned changes behind these actions bear fruit, reform momentum can certainly start to build. There are a few things to be mindful of, however. Consider the refinery upgradation plan. In a recent interaction with journalists and industry leaders, the petroleum minister allowed himself to express some annoyance that Pakistan’s refineries can only handle “the sweetest grades of crude”. This means they are using the most basic technology in their sector. His point was to underline the importance of the upgradation policy, and he emphasised that after the upgrades, Pakistan could also become an exporter of refined products. If the new rules and policy succeed in getting the refiners to do what they have not done in the past 20 years, that will be a big, positive step. Fair enough. But of the four refineries that have submitted upgradation plans, only one has the books to bear the cost. That one is Attock Refinery. The other three — National Refinery, Cynergico, and Pakistan Refinery Ltd — will struggle to raise the funds, given their books. Between the four, upgrades worth $4.2 billion have been announced. ARL’s plan is worth $600m and comes to around 1.5 times its (real) equity, which makes the plan realistic. For the others, the figures are seven to 25 times their (real) equity, which leaves one wondering about their financing plans. ARL could potentially put up 30 per cent of its equity share for the project from its own cash holdings, and the remainder would be 2.9 times its EBITDA, which is manageable. It might also need to support NRL’s financing since it owns a 25pc stake in the latter. But the other refiners will need support from multilateral lenders or an Exim bank to arrange resources for their plans. This was one reason the finance minister met officials from the US Exim Bank: to help arrange the resources the refiners, PIA, and the Reko Diq project will require. As of now, there is no reason to believe that this will create any public liabilities for the country. The refineries have been given the option to sign up for a ‘Refinery Upgradation Account’ ratified by the cabinet in August. The fund has withdrawal rules, including a requirement that projects be completed within five years, with incentives for early completion, penalties for late completion, and sales tax exemption for upgradation equipment. The rules are meant to prevent a repeat of the alleged misuse of the so-called deemed duty in the Musharraf years — when refiners were given an incentive to build stocks and they allegedly took the incentive but did not build any stock. That episode was documented in the Justice Rana Bhagwandas Judicial Commission report of 2009. This time, the funds raised from the incentives will be maintained in an account operated by the ministry, and the refiners will be able to withdraw only after showing compliance with the terms of use of this fund. If the new rules and policy succeed in getting the refiners to do what they have not done in the past 20 years, that will be a big, positive step. But much hinges on whether they can raise the financing, given the scale of the projects they have announced. Likewise, the telcos stepped forward to participate in the 5G spectrum auction after the last auction saw lukewarm participation in 2021. The bids were at or near the reserve price for most bands. Industry’s demand was that they be allowed to pay in rupees, at an exchange rate fixed at the time of the auction, and to stretch their payments over a longer period of time at Kibor plus 3pc. These concessions were granted. In return, they must introduce 5G in Islamabad first, then expand to 10 cities nationwide by 2030, and increase minimum speeds from 20mbps on 4G to 50mbps on 5G. In addition, some telcos have announced investment plans to expand their business base in Pakistan, with Jazz leading the pack through a $1bn investment plan over the next three years. These are significant steps, including the one we have not been able to discuss — the introduction of wheeling in the power sector. If they go through as envisaged, the impact will be manifest, with greater resilience in our energy supply chain against international shocks, faster communications, and more flexibility in power-provisioning arrangements. Let’s hope for the best, but remain vigilant about the pitfalls as these plans move towards implementation. The writer is a business and economy journalist.
articles.author: Khurram Husain

articles.title: Three revolutions
articles.content: THE past 250 years have seen a tsunami of revolutions — the American, the French, the Chinese, and imitating them, the Cuban. Their waves swept across the world, impacting us today and, as Chairman Mao Zedong predicted, they will affect tomorrow’s history. This year, friends of America celebrate its first 250 years; its detractors see them as its last 250 years. America enjoys the pre-eminence that capitalism promised — at a Faustian price, redeemable in US dollars. America is discomfited by Russia, a perpetual migraine; China, a recurring malaise; and Cuba, an irritating thorn in its side. A recent book by Simon Hall — Three Revolutions: Russia, China and Cuba (2025) — examines the genesis of their social upheavals. Interestingly, he links them to three writers (all American) who happened to be in the right place at the right time: John Reed, who in 1917 witnessed the ignition of the Russian Revolution; Edgar Snow, who met Mao and those who had survived the gruelling Long March of 1934-35; and Herbert Matthews, a New York Times correspondent, who in 1957 wriggled into Cuba and watched Fidel Castro’s underfunded but determined bid to depose Gen Batista. The three wrote accounts of their experiences and interaction with leaders, especially Lenin, Mao and Fidel Castro. They provided authentic, corrective insights into the social cataclysms that continue to be misunderstood by the West. In 1917, Reed sees the storming of the czar’s Winter Palace in Petrograd (now St Petersburg). Looters are prevented from despoiling the palace’s treasures and opulent furnishings by “self-appointed sentinels”, who shout: “Comrades! Don’t take anything! This is the property of the people!” Another diligent sailor guarding the Winter Palace refuses entry to a new provisional government minister and the city’s mayor. “What will you do?” the two unarmed civilians ask him. The burly sailor replies: “We will spank you, and if necessary, shoot you!” On meeting Lenin, Reed notices that he “looks through you with those terrible eyes … of being intensely interested”. Reed’s book Ten Days That Shook the World (1919) quotes Trotsky’s recollection of how Lenin, on Oct 10, 1917, scribbled a call for armed insurrection “hastily … with the gnawed end of a pencil on a sheet of paper from a child’s notebook ruled in squares”. Internecine conflicts have replaced revolutions. Lenin’s “sealed train” journey, from Switzerland across Germany and Finland to Russia, was more comfortable than the privations of the Long March. Of the 100,000 troops and party stalwarts who started from Jiangxi, only 6,000 or so reached Yan’an, 9,000 kilometres away. Edgar Snow first met Mao in 1936. He described him as a “gaunt, rather Lincolnesque figure … with a face of intellectual shrewdness”. He attributes Mao’s genius to “his uncanny ability to embody the demands of millions of his fellow citizens — above all, the peasantry”. Snow converted memories of a three-month stay in China into a book — Red Star over China (1937). It had an immeasurable impact, even in Washington’s highest circles. President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s secretary of the interior, H. Ickes, remarked presciently that “any people that can do what the Red Army did during the Long March and after” were “positively invincible”. Simon Hall’s inclusion of the Cuban revolution of 1956-59 may appear surprising until one reads how Castro achieved it. Arrested by Gen Batista’s soldiers, Castro’s life is spared by a compassionate lieutenant who tells his troops: “Don’t shoot. You can’t kill ideas”. Castro is tried and sentenced to 15 years in jail. In court, he makes a defiant speech: “I do not fear prison[.] Condemn me. It does not matter. History will absolve me.” Batista made the mistake of granting Castro an early amnesty. Castro repaid the favour by returning to Cuba from exile in Mexico. In 1956, he landed in Granma — “a creaking, leaking leisure yacht”. It was less “a landing than a shipwreck”. Harassed by Batista’s soldiers, Castro hid in the Sierra Maestra mountains — the commander of “two men, a couple of rifles and 120 rounds of ammunition”. There, he is joined by his brother Raúl, who brought five guns. Castro says, with bravado: “That makes seven. We have won the war!” Herbert Matthews interviewed Castro in his Sierra hideout, writing afterwards: “He has caught the imagination of the youth of Cuba [because] he is an educated, dedicated fanatic, a man of ideals, of courage, and of remarkable qualities of leadership.” Within three years, Castro toppled the US-supported Gen Batista. In the 21st century, internecine conflicts have replaced revolutions. Autocracies may blindfold eyes that dare to see. Revolutions, though, like tsunamis, are unpredictable. They do not wait for submissive activists who, in Lenin’s words, sit in “armchair ideas” plotting “armchair action”.
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: Fragile cryosphere
articles.content: IN contrast to last year’s catastrophic floods, this year’s monsoon flows drained through the plains of Pakistan without wreaking a major disaster. Nonetheless, the highlands of Gilgit-Baltistan and Chitral did not remain unaffected. Not too far away, Nepal experienced a horrific disaster in August. The Himalayan nation endured one of its worst catastrophes when a huge mass of glacial ice and rock collapsed down a slope in the Himalayas near the Langtang region. Within half an hour, it caused an unprecedented surge — as high as nine metres — in the Bhote Koshi/Trishuli river system. Over 1,400 people died. Thousands more went missing. A month later, a massive section of the mountainside collapsed into the swollen Kali Gandaki River after days of heavy rain, sending enormous quantities of soil, rock and debris into the water. This wave of floods and landslides caused at least two dozen deaths. Pakistan, China, India, Nepal, and Bhutan lie along the axis of disaster — the Hindu Kush-Himalaya (HKH) mountain system, also referred to as the ‘Third Pole’ because of its massive concentration of ice and glaciers. These water towers of Asia feed 10 major river systems and support the livelihoods of over two billion people in the region. Ironically, these mountains also spawn hydro-climatic disasters in the region. This explains the vulnerability of Pakistan’s highlands, as the Indus and other rivers flowing into the country draw water from these majestic mountains. The Nepal tragedy should be viewed as an early warning for Pakistan, especially for areas located in the highly fragile Hindu Kush, Karakoram and western Himalayan region. The phenomenon bears a stark resemblance to the relatively smaller-scale flash floods that occur almost yearly in the mountains of GB and KP. In its August 2026 update, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission warned that it had identified 131 potentially dangerous glacial lakes, most of them in GB and KP. The number of unfrozen PDGLs rose from 40 to 105 within a month due to higher temperatures. These findings reinforce the ominous report of the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD). Its assessment of the HKH region identified 25,614 glacial lakes across major river basins. The report also highlighted the risks linked to moraine-dammed lakes near retreating glaciers. The Nepal tragedy should be seen as a warning for Pakistan. These manifestations cannot be solely attributed to climate change, as human intervention is aggravating the impact of natural processes. The cryosphere’s health depends on several factors, including forests, vegetation, and soil stability. As forests vanish, hilly slopes are exposed and the runoff from rainwater and glacial melt increases. Flash floods become more violent and tend to carry larger amounts of debris. A study supported by the ICIMOD revealed that approximately 9,288 acres of forest were lost in Chitral between 1992 and 2009. The annual rate of deforestation accelerated from 0.14 per cent in 1992-2000 to 0.54pc in 2000-2009. Deforestation is an equally alarming trend in GB, where the forest cover has declined to 615,798 acres, comprising only 3.57pc of the total area. Population growth compounds environmental pressures. GB’s population was listed at around 881,000 in the 1998 census. By 2023, it had increased to some 1.5 million people. Similarly, Chitral recorded a population of about 516,000 in 2023. Demographic pressure amid weak land regulation has led to unregulated settlements in the dry beds of flood nullahs. A growing population increases the demand for land, which is scarce on mountain terraces and in narrow valleys. Dry nullahs are often mistaken for wasteland and used to build houses, which eventually collapse under the wrath of unforeseen gushing floods. In July 2026, Suparco highlighted the serious challenge of relentless settlement expansion along a natural glacial lake-fed stream near Gilgit city. Satellite imagery comparing construction in 2023 to that of a decade earlier indicated the rapid expansion of settlements along this natural stream. Suparco is alarmed that the narrowed channels may not safely carry high flows. The Nepal tragedy needs careful analysis to understand the parallels with the vulnerability of our cryosphere. Disaster managers should treat the catastrophe as an early warning. Residential and commercial development along mountain riverbanks, as well as deforestation in the watershed, should be strictly prohibited to avert human tragedy. The writer is a senior adviser on water governance at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute.
articles.author: Naseer Memon

articles.title: Fixing bond markets
articles.content: THE plan to deepen the domestic local currency bond market by allowing the public to trade government securities through the stock market should help address a weakness long concealed by the sovereign’s easy access to bank borrowings. Pakistan’s large government securities market lacks the depth and diversification needed to allow securities to be widely held, actively traded and efficiently priced. Banks, holding about 78pc of government securities with sovereign paper accounting for roughly 62pc of their assets, have therefore little reason to seek ‘riskier’ private borrowers. Consequently, small firms, farmers and potential homebuyers struggle to obtain credit. The proposedreformsrecognise this structural weakness. More predictable and market-based issuance, greater secondary-market liquidity, a functioning repo market and a broader investor base are all necessary. Allowing individuals to trade exchange-listed government securities through their banks should also improve access and price discovery. But can the reforms change how the market works? That requires breaking the banks’ dominance. Pension funds, insurance companies, mutual funds, retail investors, and eventually, foreign investors must become bigger participants. They need both access and incentives to hold and trade rupee securities. Secondary-market liquidity is equally important. Primary dealers should have incentives to make markets rather than merely participate in government auctions. The proposed review of the primary-dealer framework and securities-lending facility could help. The IMF should push this logic further. The government must borrow less from commercial banks. Reducing bank borrowing would force greater reliance on actual market financing, creating room for banks to lend to productive private activity. The market should also be broadened beyond government debt. The government could require SOEs to raise at least one-third of all future local currency borrowing through bonds. This would create more issuers, diversify instruments and maturities, and expose SOE borrowing to greater market scrutiny. Demand can be boosted through targeted tax incentives for investors holding local currency bonds issued by SOEs and private companies. Such incentives should encourage longer-term investment. Further, transparently priced government securities across maturities can provide benchmarks against which private companies price their own debt. Over time, this could reduce the economy’s overreliance on bank lending. That said, the government must avoid treating the bond market reform as a way to finance itself more easily. A deeper market should reduce refinancing risks, improve monetary policy transmission and redirect savings to productive investment. The measure of success cannot be the number of bonds issued. It must be who buys them, how actively they trade, how liquid the market becomes and whether businesses have better access to long-term capital.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Call centre rackets
articles.content: A NUMBER of recent raids conducted by the authorities in different cities point to the growing threat fraudulent call centres pose to the reputation of legitimate Pakistani tech businesses, as well as to the country at large. The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency said it had picked up 61 suspects from a call centre in Rawalpindi that was allegedly running foreign loan recovery scams. Earlier, the NCCIA had busted what it claimed were two call centres in Karachi owned by the same organisation. Apparently, these centres were involved in credit card scams targeting Americans. Over 50 people had been rounded up in that raid. Similar action at a dubious call centre in Islamabad a week ago resulted in over 200 people being taken into custody. Meanwhile, last year a raid at a facility in Faisalabad netted 149 people belonging to various nationalities. Fraudulent call centres are big business; criminals can extort significant amounts of foreign currency from unsuspecting victims abroad. The fraudsters offer Ponzi schemes, financial products, fake tech support and other ‘services’, through which they gain access to the victims’ financial and other sensitive data. They also target individuals in Pakistan, often impersonating bank employees, government officials, or security personnel. Pakistan is not alone as these criminal outfits are active in other countries too. In fact, India is considered as the ‘epicentre’ of the fake call centre industry. Reported raids in different cities show that the state is aware of the threat these rackets pose. Pakistan’s campaign against fraudulent call centres must continue. While genuine call centres and tech businesses must not be harassed, outfits involved in shady dealings and questionable financial transactions must be investigated and prosecuted. And while rounding up employees and small fry associated with these criminal rings may disrupt their operations, it is the masterminds behind these concerns that need to be brought to justice. The NCCIA head has said that “indiscriminate and vigorous operations” will be carried out against those involved in cyber fraud. It is hoped that the state keeps a vigilant eye on those engaged in these rackets as they use the latest technology to perpetuate fraud.
articles.author: Editorial
